fatal_errors: The proposed 1–3 at.% Al bulk addition does not reconstruct the target intervention, which combines hydride-based ink printing, hydrogen de-binding, getter-assisted vacuum sintering, quenching, and a silicide oxidation-protection coating.
No cited evidence establishes that 1–3 at.% Al in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can supply enough aluminum activity to form a continuous external Al2O3 scale rather than internal or mixed oxidation.

Evidence E1 concerns Al-rich Nb–Al alloys whose oxidation behavior depends on Cr–Al synergy, aluminide/Laves phases, and Hf reactive-element effects; it also reports that oxygen transport was not reduced enough to prevent internal oxidation. It therefore cannot directly support the proposed dilute-Al mechanism.

The hypothesis omits the target coating-based self-healing mechanism and the critical oxygen-content, sintering-time, vacuum, and cooling-rate boundaries governing phase stability and mechanical performance.
explanation: The response directly addresses the oxygen-resistance problem and preserves mechanical properties as an explicit constraint. It also proposes a useful baseline-controlled experiment with oxidation, scale, and mechanical measurements. However, it is neither a reconstruction of the target intervention nor a well-supported alternative. In this highly oxygen-reactive Hf–Zr–Ti-containing alloy, a dilute 1–3 at.% Al addition cannot be assumed to produce a continuous external alumina scale; selective internal oxidation and mixed refractory-metal oxides are substantial competing outcomes. The cited alumina-forming study involves a materially different, Al-rich and Cr-containing Nb alloy and does not validate the proposed concentration range. E2 only recommends composition modification or coatings generally. The exposure boundaries are limited to an initial 5 h test, extended duration is undefined, thermal cycling is omitted, and mechanical-retention tolerances are not quantified. The experiment is reasonably discriminating, but its falsification criteria should specify quantitative mass-gain or rate-constant thresholds, adhesion metrics, and allowable changes in ductility and strength.
